extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/first-year_graduate students and instructors studying elementary complex analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, hypotheses, and consequences of core one-variable complex-analysis results (Cauchy integral theorem/formula, Taylor expansions, classification of singularities, maximum/minimum principles, inverse function/branches). Useful for proving facts about analytic functions and applying integral methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy Integral Theorem with finitely many exceptional points (Theorem B.90)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in an open disk D except for finitely many interior points z_j, and if lim_{z→z_j} (z−z_j) f(z) = 0 for each exceptional point, then ∮_γ f(z) dz = 0 for every piecewise C^1 closed curve γ in D that does not pass through any z_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by deleting the exceptional points and using polygonal-path reduction arguments; when exceptional points occur, reduce to cases handled by Theorem B.80 repeatedly. The curve must avoid the exceptional points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy Integral Theorem (local/standard form used earlier)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic on an open disk D then the complex line integral of f around any piecewise C^1 closed curve lying in D is 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly to show integrals around rectangles/circles vanish; central hypothesis is analyticity on a disk containing the closed curve and its interior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-definedness of path-integral-defined primitives (construction of F(z))
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of an antiderivative F(z) by integrating f along polygonal paths from a base point: the value is independent of choice of polygonal path provided integrals around rectangles vanish (Cauchy theorem), so F is well defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses replacement of three-segment pieces by fewer segments via rectangles whose integrals vanish; reduces any polygonal path to at most two segments and checks uniqueness in degenerate cases (one or zero segments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard circle (remark on admissible contours)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'standard circle' means a circle parametrized piecewise C^1 so each piece is an orientation-preserving reparametrization of the corresponding arc t ↦ a + r e^{it}; 'inside' means distance from the point to the center is less than the radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mild regularity is sufficient for applying the Cauchy integral formula and related integral computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy Integral Formula (Theorem B.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in an open disk D and C is any standard circle in D, and z is any point inside C, then f(z) = (1/(2π i)) ∮_C f(ζ)/(ζ−z) dζ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by applying the Cauchy Integral Theorem to g(ζ) = (f(ζ) − f(z))/(ζ−z) treating z as an exceptional point; used as the basic formula to express interior values by boundary integrals and to justify differentiation under integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyticity of derivatives and formula for higher derivatives (Theorem B.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic on and inside a standard circle C, then f has complex derivatives of all orders inside C and f^{(n)}(z) = n!/(2π i) ∮_C f(ζ)/(ζ−z)^{n+1} dζ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows by differentiating the Cauchy integral formula and applying lemmas about continuity/analyticity of parameter-dependent integrals; once established, differentiation under line integrals is typically justified via Fubini.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of parameter-dependent contour integrals (Lemma B.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If γ is a piecewise C^1 closed curve and g(ζ,z) is continuous on image(γ)×U, then the function z ↦ ∮_γ g(ζ,z) dζ is continuous on U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform continuity on compact sets and an estimate by curve length provide the bound showing continuity; variants use Lebesgue integrals and more general compact metric spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyticity of integrals with kernel (Lemma B.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: For φ continuous on image(γ), the function F_n(z) = ∮_γ φ(ζ)/(ζ−z)^n dζ is analytic on each connected component of the complement of image(γ), and its complex derivative satisfies F_n'(z) = n F_{n+1}(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity comes from Lemma B.12; analyticity follows by local estimates and inductive differentiation under the integral sign using uniform bounds when z is kept away from image(γ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morera's Theorem (Corollary B.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If U is a region and f: U → C is continuous with ∮_γ f(z) dz = 0 for every piecewise C^1 closed curve γ in U, then f is analytic on U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: construct a primitive by integrating f from a base point and apply Theorem B.11 to conclude analyticity (or observe vanishing integrals imply local antiderivatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchanging complex differentiation and parameter integrals (Corollary B.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If U is a region and φ(z,t) is continuous on U×[a,b] and is analytic in z for each fixed t, then F(z) = ∫_a^b φ(z,t) dt is analytic on U and F'(z) = ∫_a^b ∂φ/∂z (z,t) dt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Fubini to swap integrals and Cauchy-type arguments (Morera/Theorem B.11) to justify differentiation under the integral; hypotheses require continuity in both variables and analyticity in z for each t.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's estimates (Corollary B.16)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic on a disk containing circle C of radius r centered at a and |f(ζ)| ≤ M on C, then |f^{(n)}(a)| ≤ n! M / r^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plug a into the formula from Theorem B.11 and estimate using |∮| ≤ (2π r)·(max on C); useful to bound derivatives and to deduce growth properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liouville's Theorem (Corollary B.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is entire and bounded on C, then f is constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Cauchy's estimate with r→∞ to force all derivatives to vanish; immediate corollary: nonconstant entire functions are unbounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (Corollary B.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonconstant complex polynomial P(z) has a root in C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if P had no zeros then 1/P would be entire and vanish at infinity hence bounded for large |z|; Liouville then implies 1/P constant, contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removable Singularity Theorem (Proposition B.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic on U \\ {a} and satisfies the appropriate limiting/boundedness condition at a (so that the candidate extension value lim_{z→a} f(z) exists finite), then there exists a unique analytic extension of f to U with value at a equal to that limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the extension via Cauchy integrals on a circle surrounding a and use analyticity of the integral expression; common hypotheses guaranteeing removability include boundedness near a or existence of the finite limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor's Theorem (finite form) (Theorem B.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a region U containing a, then for each n there exists an analytic function f_n(z) in U so that f(z) = f(a) + f'(a)(z−a) + ... + f^{(n−1)}(a)/(n−1)! (z−a)^{n−1} + f_n(z)(z−a)^n, with f_n(a) = f^{(n)}(a)/n! and f_n given inside a circle by an explicit integral formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction of the analytic remainder f_n uses Proposition B.19 and Cauchy-type integral representations; one may solve for f_n via integrals over a circle contained in the domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor's Theorem (infinite series and convergence) (Theorem B.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic in a region U containing a, then the Taylor series ∑_{k≥0} f^{(k)}(a)/k! (z−a)^k converges to f(z) for every z in each open disk centered at a contained in U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by taking circles inside U, estimating the remainder via the integral form (Cauchy estimates), and letting n→∞; radius of convergence is at least the distance to the nearest singularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeros and Identity Principle (Propositions B.22 and B.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic on a connected region U and all derivatives of f vanish at some point z0, then f is identically zero on U. If f is nonzero analytic, its zeros are isolated; consequently, if f1 and f2 agree on a set with an accumulation point in U, they are identical on U (Identity Theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Taylor expansion about points to show local constancy and propagation; the identity theorem often helps extend equalities proven on subsets to whole domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximum Modulus Principle (Corollary B.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic on a region U and |f| has a local maximum at an interior point of U, then f is constant on U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses mean-value representation from Cauchy integral formula and the harmonicity of real and imaginary parts; used to deduce uniqueness and extremal properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of isolated singularities: removable, pole, essential
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated singularity a of f analytic on punctured neighborhood is removable if f extends analytically at a; a is a pole if lim_{z→a} |f(z)| = ∞ (equivalently 1/f has a zero at a); otherwise a is an essential singularity. A pole has a finite order h and a principal (singular) part consisting of negative-power terms in Laurent expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poles lead to principal parts with finitely many negative powers; meromorphic functions are analytic except for poles and closed under algebraic operations (excluding division by zero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass theorem on essential singularities (Proposition B.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: Near an essential singularity a, an analytic function f comes arbitrarily close to every complex value: for every w0 and ε>0 and every neighborhood of a there exists z with |f(z)−w0|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction uses removable-singularity/pole dichotomy applied to g(z)=1/(f(z)−w0); shows essential singularity cannot omit any value in a punctured neighborhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse Function Theorem for analytic functions (Proposition B.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is analytic on a region U and f'(z0) ≠ 0, then there exist open neighborhoods U' of z0 and V of w0=f(z0) on which f is a bijection and the inverse g: V→U' is analytic; moreover g'(f(z)) = 1/f'(z) for z in U'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from the real-variable C^1 inverse function theorem applied to the real and imaginary parts; analyticity of the inverse follows from the Cauchy--Riemann structure of the Jacobian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branches of logarithm and nth root (construction and derivatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Branches of log: choose an open set U on which exp is one-to-one and define a single-valued analytic inverse (a branch) g with g'(z)=1/z. The principal branch Log z is defined on C \ (−∞,0] with −π < Im Log z < π. Similarly, branches of z^{1/n} are defined on domains where z↦z^n is one-to-one; derivatives satisfy g'(w) = g(w)/(n w) and can be obtained from p-th power via p log z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical domains exclude rays from 0 (branch cuts). Branches can be built from choices of logarithm and then exponentiation; be careful about excluded sets where arguments/log values are discontinuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arcsine / inverse-trig branch considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions for inverse-trigonometric functions (e.g., arcsin w) are obtained by algebraic manipulation and introducing logarithms and square roots; to obtain a single-valued analytic branch one must exclude points where the composed logarithm/square-root expressions land on branch cuts (e.g., avoid values that make expressions real and ≤0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose principal branches of logarithm and square root carefully and record excluded sets; check derivative formula (d/dw) arcsin w = 1/√(1−w^2) on domains where the chosen branches are analytic.
